PGO: The Postgres Operator from Crunchy Data
PGO, the Postgres Operator from Crunchy Data, gives you a **declarative Postgres** solution that automatically manages your PostgreSQL clusters.

Designed for your GitOps workflows, it is easy to get started with Postgres on Kubernetes with PGO. Within a few moments, you can have a production-grade Postgres cluster complete with high availability, disaster recovery, and monitoring, all over secure TLS communications. Even better, PGO lets you easily customize your Postgres cluster to tailor it to your workload!
Have questions or looking for help? Join our Discord group.
To build the various containers required by PGO, please see the build instructions found in the components directory of this repository.

These images are built using packages developed by the PostgreSQL Global Development Group (PGDG). Each subdirectory contains a `README` file describing how to build each of the various containers required by PGO.

Crunchy Data makes PGO available as the orchestration behind Crunchy Postgres for Kubernetes. Crunchy Postgres for Kubernetes is the integrated product that includes PostgreSQL, PGO and a collection of PostgreSQL tools and extensions that includes the various open source components listed in the documentation.

We call it a "wildcard container image" because the same base image becomes whatever the project needs. It is a host in a box, stateful by design: the container filesystem holds the state, restarts preserve the environment, and image upgrades are handled as migrations. See State and Upgrades.

Infinite OS starts as a single Go binary on a lightweight Debian base, using about 80MB of RAM. That makes running several small environments side by side practical. It is also the model behind our own cloud hosting: many Infinite OS environments instead of one large shared-hosting server.
> **Using an AI coding agent?** Point it at `SKILL.md`. It maps the dashboard, CLI, and REST API, and covers the core deployment workflows.
Your own application works the same way: clone it into the environment, install its runtime, create its database, and map it to a hostname. `SKILL.md` has examples for PHP, Node.js, Python, and more.

Infinite OS is also not a PaaS such as Coolify, Dokku, or CapRover. Those tools manage deployments and containers; Infinite OS is the hosting environment inside one container. Our sibling project Infinite Ez handles the multi-environment layer.

Port `1618` serves the dashboard and API. The example binds it to `127.0.0.1` so the setup wizard is not exposed. On a production server, deploy through a PaaS: we recommend Infinite Ez, which makes the setup straightforward.

Masquerade is two things. It is a TCP proxy that sits between your Postgres Database and client and proxies data back and forth. The proxy listens to all messages sent from the database to the client and provides a hook for users to modify data in-transit and before being received by the client. Second, it is a masker. It has built-in functionality that can mask sensitive data in the database so that it cannot be seen by the client.

Masquerade works out of the box and you can start masking your data immediately. Simply run the proxy (see below) and begin issues SQL queries as you would normally do and you'll see the masked reults.

For **remote access**, terminate TLS — set `tls_cert`+`tls_key`, or front with nginx/caddy/traefik and keep the loopback bind. Serving plaintext on a routable address is refused unless you explicitly set `allow_insecure_http: true` (or pass `--insecure-http`) — see Security.

**Jump to:** Why · Features · Architecture · Install · Quickstart · Operators & auth · Deployment · Endpoints · Status · Production readiness · Security

- **PKI lifecycle** — per-operator CAs encrypted at rest in SQLite under a process-wide AES-256-GCM master key (envelope encryption per ADR 0002); per-host certs signed via `slackhq/nebula/cert`; blocklist-backed revocation. New operators get a default CA auto-provisioned on first sign-in.

- **CA rotation** — when a CA approaches expiry (≤20% lifetime left), a warning badge appears in the UI; operators rotate manually with one click or opt into background auto-rotation. Existing host certificates remain valid until natural expiry. Details in ADR 0008.

- **Per-host advanced overrides** — `listen_host`, `mtu`, `tun_device`, `punchy`, `punchy_respond`, `unsafe_routes` opt-in per host without touching the network default. A lighthouse can add `extra_endpoints`, such as its LAN address for peers behind the same NAT. `nebula_version` names the Nebula release of a host without an agent, such as a mobile client; agents report their host's release and OS themselves, and the host list shows it. Nebula 1.12 tuning (`routines`, offloads, thread pinning, the local API control socket) renders only for hosts whose release and OS support it; see docs/agent.md.

- **Gateways to non-Nebula networks** — `unsafe_networks` on a host signs the prefixes it may route for into its certificate, the provider half of another host's `unsafe_routes`. Nebula authorizes routing on the certificate, so without it the gateway silently refuses to route and peers drop the traffic before any firewall rule runs. Editing it is a certificate-bound change, so the gateway re-enrolls on its next poll and the new certificate carries the prefix. See docs/agent.md.

Non-admin operators see and manage only the CAs they own; admins see all. Hosts enrolled under a tenant CA receive **that** CA's certificate, not the default one.
